_purpose: Checklist manifest for design-review mode, parallel in spirit to rubric_manifest.json but for evaluating a NEW FEATURE PROPOSAL against a target system, not auditing an existing repo's debt. Every check here is mandatory on every design-review run — a proposal that hasn't addressed a dimension yet doesn't excuse skipping the check, it means the check's answer is 'open-question' or 'risk (missing)', recorded honestly rather than omitted. There is deliberately no system_type_overrides table: unlike the debt-audit manifest, applicability here doesn't vary by what kind of repo the target is, it varies by what the proposal actually touches — and that's a per-instance judgment (not-applicable status on a specific check instance), not a manifest-level exemption.

checks.summary: Does the proposal respect the target repo's existing module/service boundaries, or does it reach across a boundary the codebase otherwise keeps closed? Cite the specific existing boundary (package structure, API gateway, ownership doc) being crossed or respected.
Does this duplicate a capability that already exists in the target system(s) under a different name? Grep for existing components with overlapping responsibility before assuming this is net-new.
Every new/changed persisted field, table, or event schema: is there a migration plan for existing data, and is backward compatibility for in-flight readers/writers addressed?
Data ownership: does the proposal introduce a new source of truth for data another system already owns, or duplicate/fork state that should stay canonical in one place?

Does the proposal state an expected load/scale (QPS, data volume, growth rate), and does the target system's current architecture (from the deterministic signals + reading) actually support it? Flag hardcoded capacity assumptions the proposal is silent on.
New/changed surface (endpoint, queue topic, UI action): is authN/authZ addressed, and does it match the target system's existing security boundary pattern rather than inventing a new one?
Does the proposal touch data with sensitivity implications (PII, financial, regulated) without naming the applicable compliance requirement or data-handling constraint?
Observability plan: does the proposal name what will be logged/metered/traced/alerted on for the new surface, and who owns responding to it?
Failure modes: does the proposal describe what happens when a dependency it introduces is slow/unavailable, and is there a rollback or feature-flag path if the rollout goes wrong?
Existing API/consumer compatibility: does this proposal break an existing contract (request/response shape, event schema, CLI flag) that another team or system depends on?
If this spans multiple repos/systems, is the cross-repo sequencing/versioning explicit (which side deploys first, how is the in-between state handled)?
Does the proposal name the infra/operational cost implications (new service, storage growth, third-party API spend) of this change, proportionate to its actual scope?
Does the proposal name at least one alternative approach it considered and explain why it wasn't chosen, or does it present one option with no visible tradeoff analysis?
Does the proposal describe how correctness will be validated pre- and post-launch (test strategy, staged rollout, experiment/metric to watch)?
Are the stated objectives and KPIs internally coherent (no ambiguous/contradictory targets), and does each objective have at least one KPI that would actually detect whether it succeeded?

For each objective, is there a traceable architecture/roadmap element responsible for delivering it, sized proportionately to how the proposal itself ranks that objective's importance? Flag objectives that are given top billing but the thinnest design/roadmap treatment, or KPIs with no architecture element that owns hitting them.

Does the proposal have a coherent narrative flow (agenda/table-of-contents matches what's actually presented, section order builds logically, no duplicated/near-duplicate slides), and does each slide/section have a single clear takeaway rather than mixing several distinct ideas?

Is information density/verbosity appropriate for the actual audience (a time-boxed senior review committee, not necessarily deep specialists in every named technology), and does implementation-level plumbing crowd out room for risk/tradeoff discussion rather than being pushed to an appendix?

Presence/absence checklist against the standard sections a mature design proposal usually carries: deployment strategy, rollout/rollback plan, phased plan, testing strategy, observability/monitoring, ownership/on-call, security review, cost, alternatives, success metrics. This checks whether a section exists at all (signals the presenter thought about it) — the CONTENT quality within a present section is graded by the other dimensions, not here, so don't double-penalize the same gap twice.

Identify what the proposal's OWN content implies is its single most load-bearing design element or dependency — the thing that, if wrong or missing, breaks the core value proposition (often visible only from cross-referencing findings from other dimensions, e.g. a diagram dependency with no code/ticket backing it, per dependencies-and-integration.b). Then check whether the deck's narrative actually returns to it — in Objectives, Risks & Mitigation, and the Roadmap — proportionate to how much rests on it, or whether it appears once (often buried in a diagram with no accompanying text) while lower-stakes, better-understood, or purely internal implementation detail gets dedicated, even duplicated, slides. A proposal can be well-organized (passing check .a) and still tell an inverted story where its riskiest, most critical thread gets the least narrative weight.
Are cross-team/cross-repo/cross-system dependencies this proposal relies on explicitly named, with any blocking sequencing called out (e.g. 'requires Team X's API to ship first')?

For every cross-system guarantee/gate the proposal's diagram or text claims ("system X won't proceed until Y is true" — a readiness check, a validation gate, an enforced precondition), verify there's an actual enforcement point wired up on the CONSUMING side, not just a capability that exists on the providing side. A server endpoint nobody calls, or a diagram arrow with no corresponding integration ticket/code on the other end, delivers none of the guarantee the proposal claims — check the provider's own docs/tickets for named consumers and their status, and treat an unverifiable or unticketed consumer as a real gap, not an assumed detail. This is systems-thinking, not a single-repo check: think like a domain expert tracing how the systems on both sides of an integration actually depend on each other, not just what one side built.
